name: Maya Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the install crew on a new primary school that's built almost entirely from mass timber. That means big wall and floor panels made of glued layers of wood, cut to the millimetre in a factory and delivered on lorries. My crew of six guides them off the crane, screws them together and seals the joints. I'm on site at seven checking the delivery order against the crane plan, because if panel 14 comes before panel 12 we're stuck with a lorry in the road and a very angry neighbour.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love how fast it goes up. We did a whole floor in four days last month, and the kids from the old school came to watch through the fence. I use AI every day, for checking the lift sequence, writing method statements, even asking it how to fix a panel that's arrived slightly warped. What wears me out is the weather, you can't lift a panel in high wind, so one gusty day wrecks the whole week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, it's a good tool and that's what it stays. At work I'd still use it for the paperwork and nobody would care. Online I might post something like, turns out the hype was hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little surprised, because I see what it does every day and it keeps getting better. But it wouldn't change much for us. Jonas, my husband, is a physio, so his work is all hands on people anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as now. Keep using the tools, keep the crew, keep putting money into our index fund each month like we have for ten years. Maybe I'd do the course on reading factory machine files that I've been meaning to do, because it'd help with warped panels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same as today, which is a good place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years of an index fund. How did that start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad was a carpenter and never had a pension, he worked till his knees gave up. I promised myself I wouldn't do that. So since I was thirty-three, a fixed amount goes in on payday before I can spend it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the one part of the job you'd want AI to help with more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The weather forecast for lifting days. If something could tell me on Monday which days will be safe to lift, I'd plan the whole week around it. That's real money saved.

S0.say: She'd say AI is a good tool and that's what it stays, maybe posting that the hype turned out to be hype. At work she'd keep using it for paperwork.
S0.think: Privately she'd be a little surprised, since she sees AI improving every day. It wouldn't change much for her family, with her husband in hands-on physiotherapy.
S0.do: Keeps running her crew and using AI tools daily, while continuing monthly index fund payments. Takes the course on reading factory machine files she's been meaning to do.
S0.feel: Calm, same as today, which feels like a good place to be.
S0.quote: My dad was a carpenter and never had a pension, he worked till his knees gave up.
S0.fieldNote: Maya is a daily AI user who works in a factory-linked, fast-moving part of construction. Her financial discipline comes from watching her father, which she tells as a clear story. She'd be the least changed by a plateau.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what's already happening in my corner of the trade, just spread wider. I'd tell the younger ones, learn the digital side and you'll never be short of work. Online I'd post photos of our panel jobs to show what it looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think it's good for me. The factory side of timber building is growing, and they need people who know how panels behave on site. My crew might get smaller, but I'd be in a better seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first six months I'd talk to the panel factory about a job planning installs, because they've hinted before. I'd do the machine files course properly, around twelve hundred, paid myself. And I'd put a bit extra into the fund, maybe in companies building this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of buzz. Like the morning of a big lift when the wind's dropped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your crew of six?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring Kemi with me if I could, she's quick on the digital stuff. The others, I'd help them find other site work, and round here that's not hard. It's a market, people move, I'd rather be honest about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd blame if your crew shrank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. It's cheaper and faster, the clients want it, the schools want to open sooner. You can't blame a school for wanting its kids out of a leaky portable cabin.

S1.say: She'd say steady change is already happening in timber building and just spreading wider. She'd tell younger workers to learn the digital side and post photos of panel jobs online.
S1.think: Privately she thinks it's good for her, as factory timber grows and needs people who know how panels behave on site. Her crew might shrink but she'd be in a better position.
S1.do: Approaches the panel factory about an install planning job within six months and pays about twelve hundred for a machine files course. Puts extra into her investments, including companies building this technology.
S1.feel: Calm with a bit of buzz, like a big lift morning after the wind drops.
S1.quote: You can't blame a school for wanting its kids out of a leaky portable cabin.
S1.fieldNote: Her centre outlook shows clearly: she blames nobody and sees the market as natural. She moves early and confidently towards the factory side. She'd try to take one colleague with her and is frank that others would have to find their own way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is big and fast, and people should make a plan this week, not next year. I'd say it calmly, because panicking helps nobody. Online I'd share what I know about what robots can actually do on a site right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried, but mostly for other people. We've got savings, the fund, and Jonas's work is the kind people still want a human for, at least for a while. If AI can do almost anything, I'd be out of a job in a couple of years, but I'd have a cushion and I'd want to be inside the change, not outside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd move part of our fund into the companies making the robots and the AI, because if it's that fast, that's where the money goes. I'd try to get a job with whoever's deploying robots on timber sites, maybe running their first jobs. We'd stop the plan to move house and keep our current mortgage, which is small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A tight feeling, but I'd be busy, and busy helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want to be inside the change. What does that look like on a Monday morning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably me in a hi-vis next to a robot arm that's lifting a panel, with a tablet, checking it's doing it right. And a lot of phone calls to the factory. Honestly, it doesn't sound that different from now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Noor and Elias?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor's twelve, she'd be worried about her friends' parents, because she's like that. I'd tell her we're okay and that we'll help people if we can. Elias would ask if the robot can build him a treehouse.

S2.say: She'd say calmly that this is big and fast and people should plan this week. Online she'd share what she knows about what robots can really do on sites today.
S2.think: Privately she'd worry mostly for others, since she has savings, investments and a husband whose work still needs a human for a while. She'd expect to lose her job in a couple of years but would want to be inside the change.
S2.do: Moves part of the family's investments into robot and AI companies in the first month. Seeks a job with a firm deploying robots on timber sites and cancels plans to move house, keeping their small mortgage.
S2.feel: Uneasy and tight, but kept steady by being busy.
S2.quote: Honestly, it doesn't sound that different from now.
S2.fieldNote: Secure, adaptive and already working with factory-made panels, Maya stays uneasy rather than alarmed even with two years' warning. Her first move is to invest in the change itself. She notices her daughter's concern for other families, which hints at the social cost she doesn't dwell on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good amount of time to get ahead, if you use it. I'd encourage people at work to learn something new every year. I'd be fairly upbeat in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to move twice. First into planning installs for the factory, then into whatever's next, maybe running robot crews. I'm not worried about myself, I'm curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd take the job at the panel factory and do two short courses, one on machine files and one on robot site safety. I'd start a small side business with Kemi doing install checks for other builders using timber, weekends, to see if it grows. And I'd keep paying into the fund and the mortgage as normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Interested more than anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd grab the first thing inside the change. With five I can choose, build a little business, take Kemi with me. Five years means I'm not just reacting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not worried about yourself. Is there anyone you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother. He drives a delivery van, and that's going early in any of these. I'd probably help him with money for a course, and Jonas wouldn't mind.

S3.say: She'd say five years is a good amount of time to get ahead if you use it. She'd be upbeat in public and encourage colleagues to learn something new every year.
S3.think: Privately she thinks five years lets her move twice, first into factory install planning and then into running robot crews. She's curious rather than worried for herself.
S3.do: Takes a job at the panel factory and does two short courses on machine files and robot site safety in the first year. Starts a weekend side business with a colleague doing install checks for other builders and keeps up investment and mortgage payments.
S3.quote: Five years means I'm not just reacting.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Maya is not just safe but enterprising, building a side business. She reveals a worry close to home, her brother's delivery van job, and offers practical family help. Her calm is grounded in savings, skills and a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse not to get ready. I'd push the company to start training now. I'd be pretty relaxed in public, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is long enough that I'd probably do two different careers in it. At fifty-three I'd have a paid-off house, a decent fund, and I'd be choosing what I do, not being told. That's my dad's story turned the other way round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on site for a few more years, because I like it. Around year three I'd move into the factory side, then build up the side business with Kemi. I'd keep paying into the fund every month, maybe a little more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit proud, even, that I set things up to be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd move to the factory in the first six months. Why wait here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because there's no rush. I'd rather enjoy a few more years of watching a school go up in four days a floor. When it's time, I'll move, and I'll have saved more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want for Noor and Elias by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor would be twenty-two, Elias nineteen. I'd want them to know how to make something with their hands and how to talk to the machines. And to save from their first payslip, like I told myself I would.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is plenty and there's no excuse not to get ready. She'd push the company to start training now and would sound genuinely relaxed.
S4.think: Privately she expects to have two careers in the decade and reach fifty-three with a paid-off house and a solid fund. She sees it as her father's story turned around.
S4.do: Stays on site a few more years for enjoyment, then moves to the factory side around year three. Builds up the side business with her colleague and keeps paying into investments, slightly increasing them.
S4.feel: Calm, and a little proud of having set things up to be ready.
S4.quote: That's my dad's story turned the other way round.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she even slows down, choosing to enjoy site work longer. Her father's story runs through the whole interview as her motivation. She wants her children to combine hand skills with machine skills and saving habits.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, but more for the people around me than for me, my brother, half my crew. What would help is quick, short training that people can actually get into, and some money from somewhere to carry them through. For me, honestly, being allowed to get on with it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the weather. I'm joking, a bit. But even the best robot can't lift a panel in a gale, so somebody still has to make the call on the day.

headlineQuote: Even the best robot can't lift a panel in a gale, so somebody still has to make the call on the day.
portrait: Maya Haddad is a 43-year-old install lead on a mass-timber primary school, married to a physiotherapist, with a daughter of twelve and a son of nine. She uses AI every day, invests monthly because her carpenter father never had a pension, and already works with factory-cut panels. She is calm across the plateau and steady change, only uneasy under AGI in two years, and calm again with five or ten years to move into the factory side and a weekend business. She blames nobody and sees the shift as a market she intends to ride.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, though mainly for her brother and her crew rather than herself.
whatWouldHelp: Short, quick training people can actually get into, money to carry them through, and for herself, being allowed to get on with it.
